question.text: The MAIN tax benefit of using a GIFT-IFSC feeder fund (as opposed to a Mauritius/Singapore feeder) is:

answer.text: GIFT-IFSC income qualifies for 100% tax holiday under Section 80LA of the Income-tax Act for any 10 consecutive years in a 15-year block, on specified income
GIFT-IFSC funds are fully exempt from SEBI regulations
GIFT-IFSC feeders face lower GST than Mauritius feeders
GIFT-IFSC allows leverage up to 10x unlike offshore

explanation.text: The Logic: Under Section 80LA of the Income-tax Act, eligible IFSC units may claim a 100% deduction on specified income (including fund-management income) for any 10 consecutive assessment years chosen within the first 15 years of operation. For a GIFT-IFSC feeder this is a very material benefit relative to a Mauritius or Singapore feeder, whose tax treatment rests on treaty residency and substance rather than a domestic holiday. GIFT-IFSC fund management is regulated by IFSCA under the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations framework. The Trap: Option B is false — GIFT-IFSC is regulated by IFSCA, not exempt. Option C invents a GST advantage that depends on supply rules, not a feeder-fund feature. Option D fabricates a leverage uplift; leverage limits follow IFSCA norms. Note: Section 80LA, the 100% tax holiday, and the 10-years-in-15-years window are not explicitly set out in the cited XIX-E (Category III AIF Managers) workbook pages, which note general IFSC tax benefits and IFSCA/FME feeder-registration concepts. The framing above reflects the general Indian tax-law position on IFSC units.
